results.summary_before: This is a true random number generator that uses a noise source sampled by a digital circuit and conditions the data with SHA-256 to produce cryptographic-quality random numbers. It supports raw entropy and hashed output modes, with built-in health tests, and transmits results via UART. It requires a UART terminal and optionally an oscilloscope for debugging. The design is notable for its cryptographic conditioning and health monitoring.
results.summary: This is a true random number generator that samples a noise source with a digital circuit and conditions the data using SHA-256 to produce cryptographic-quality random numbers. It supports raw entropy output for analysis and hashed output for secure applications, with built-in health tests such as the repetition count test. A state machine controls data collection, processing, and transmission of results over UART. Testing requires a UART terminal, and optionally an oscilloscope for debugging the noise source.

results.summary_before: This is a Verilog driver for the Adafruit 2.13-inch e-ink display, which uses the SSD1680 chipset. It generates eight simple patterns in real time and sends them via SPI, with a special mode to copy SRAM contents to the display. It requires the specific e-ink display and a bundle of jumper wires to connect to the PMOD. The design is notable for its low memory overhead and ability to put the display into deep sleep while retaining the image.

results.summary_before: This project generates Linear Timecode (LTC) for audio and video synchronization, using counters to track time and frame count and emitting 80-bit biphase-mark-coded frames on a single pin. It adds I2C control for setting timecode and user bits, with framerate, drop-frame, color-frame, and background-format flags on ui[2..7], and debug outputs including a seven-segment framerate display. It is designed to work with the Tiny Tapeout Audio PMOD for line-level output, and I2C requires pull-ups and a host such as a Bus Pirate. This is a v2 revision of a design previously taped out on several shuttles, and the documentation is detailed about wiring and testing.

results.summary_before: This is a purely combinational 8-bit prime number detector that uses a 256-bit lookup table to identify primes from 0 to 255. The lower hex nibble of the input number is displayed on the 7-segment display, and the decimal point lights up when the number is prime. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout demo board's DIP switches and 7-segment display. The design is notable for its zero-latency operation and minimal gate count of about 100 gates.
